title: Troponin
subtitle: Myocardial injury, serial change and assay limitations
summary: Myocardial injury, serial change and assay limitations
introduction: Use the assay-specific 99th-centile upper reference limit and the validated local 0/1-hour, 0/2-hour or other pathway. Troponin indicates myocardial injury; myocardial infarction requires a compatible rise/fall plus clinical evidence of ischaemia.

rows.name: Below assay cut-off
rows.referenceRange: RVH hs-troponin T: female 99th centile ≤9 ng/L; male 99th centile ≤17 ng/L; lower reporting limit 5 ng/L
notes: A single low result only rules out MI when the validated pathway permits it, taking account of symptom onset and sampling time. It does not rule out unstable angina, PE, aortic disease or other causes of chest pain.

rows.name: Above 99th centile
rows.referenceRange: RVH hs-troponin T above local 99th centile: female >9 ng/L; male >17 ng/L. Presentation result ≥52 ng/L is high risk in the local ACS guidance.
notes: Possible causes include type 1 MI, supply–demand mismatch, tachyarrhythmia, heart failure, myocarditis, PE, sepsis, renal disease, stroke, trauma or strenuous exercise.

rows.name: Rise or fall
rows.referenceRange: RVH hs-troponin T delta: ≥5 ng/L at 1 hour is significant; 3–4 ng/L warrants observation/further sampling; >20% change at 3 hours with one value above the 99th centile is significant
notes: Dynamic change supports acute injury. Chronic stable elevation is common in CKD and structural heart disease, but a new rise/fall can still represent acute MI.

urgentFindings: Ongoing or recurrent ischaemic-type pain (central pressure/tightness, exertional pain, sweating, vomiting or radiation), regardless of an initial troponin.
ST elevation/depression, dynamic T-wave change, ventricular arrhythmia, syncope, hypotension or acute heart-failure signs.
A rising troponin above the assay threshold with symptoms or ECG evidence of ischaemia.
overrides: Use the reporting laboratory’s reference ranges and compare with previous results, symptoms, observations, medication and fluid status.

commonPatterns.title: Type 1 MI picture
findings: Troponin above the 99th centile with a significant rise/fall on serial sampling
Ischaemic-type symptoms or ECG changes (ST elevation/depression, dynamic T-wave change)
interpretation: Supports acute plaque rupture/thrombosis (type 1 MI) rather than a chronic or non-coronary cause
The diagnosis of MI needs the biochemical rise/fall plus clinical evidence of ischaemia, not troponin alone
actions: Treat as time-critical per local ACS/chest pain pathway regardless of a single reassuring earlier result (see urgent findings)
Obtain serial ECGs and repeat troponin per the validated local pathway timing
Arrange urgent medical review; do not wait for a further result if ongoing ischaemic symptoms or ECG changes are present

commonPatterns.title: Type 2 MI / supply–demand mismatch picture
findings: Troponin above the 99th centile, with or without a dynamic rise/fall
A precipitant such as tachyarrhythmia, severe hypotension, severe anaemia, hypoxia or sepsis rather than typical ischaemic chest pain
interpretation: Reflects myocardial oxygen supply–demand imbalance rather than primary coronary plaque rupture, though the two can co-exist and are not always easy to separate clinically
Still requires clinical correlation — a raised troponin should not be dismissed as 'just' type 2 without considering ACS
actions: Identify and treat the precipitant (rate control, resuscitation, correct anaemia/hypoxia, treat sepsis)
Request FBC and U&E to assess for anaemia and renal function as contributing factors (see further testing)
Arrange medical review, particularly if the precipitant is not readily identified or the patient remains symptomatic

commonPatterns.title: Chronic stable elevation picture
findings: Troponin persistently above the 99th centile on repeat testing
Known CKD or structural heart disease
interpretation: Chronic stable elevation is common in CKD and structural heart disease and does not by itself indicate acute MI
A new rise/fall from this chronic baseline can still represent acute injury, so previous results are important context
actions: Compare with any previous troponin results where available to establish the patient's own baseline
Continue to assess symptoms and ECG on their own merits rather than dismissing a raised result as 'baseline' without comparison
Arrange medical review if there is a new symptomatic presentation or the result is higher than the patient's known baseline

commonPatterns.title: Possible myocarditis / pericarditis picture
findings: Chest pain, often pleuritic or positional, sometimes preceded by a viral illness
Diffuse ECG changes rather than a single-territory pattern
interpretation: Myocarditis and pericarditis can raise troponin through direct myocardial inflammation rather than coronary thrombosis
Can be difficult to distinguish from ACS on troponin and ECG alone; both need urgent assessment
actions: Ask about preceding viral symptoms, pericarditic features (positional/pleuritic pain, relief sitting forward) and exercise history
Obtain a 12-lead ECG and treat as a time-critical presentation while ACS remains a differential (see urgent findings)
Arrange urgent medical review for further assessment, which may include echocardiography

commonPatterns.title: PE-associated troponin rise
findings: Hypoxia, tachycardia, pleuritic chest pain or risk factors for venous thromboembolism
interpretation: Right ventricular strain from a significant pulmonary embolism can raise troponin and is a marker of higher-risk PE, not just an incidental finding
Should not be assumed to be cardiac in origin without considering PE, particularly with hypoxia or risk factors
actions: Assess PE risk factors and consider a validated PE risk score as part of the wider assessment
Request D-dimer if clinically appropriate, and treat as time-critical if haemodynamically unstable (see further testing)
Arrange urgent medical review; escalate directly if there is haemodynamic compromise or severe hypoxia

commonPatterns.title: Too-early / non-diagnostic sample
findings: Troponin below the assay cut-off or the 99th centile
Symptom onset very recent relative to the sample, or sampling timing outside the validated pathway
interpretation: A single low troponin only excludes MI when the validated local pathway's timing rules are met — an early sample can be falsely reassuring
A low troponin does not exclude unstable angina, PE, aortic dissection or other causes of chest pain
actions: Check the time from symptom onset and confirm this fits the validated 0/1-hour, 0/2-hour or other local pathway before treating the result as reassuring
Arrange repeat troponin at the pathway-defined interval if the timing criteria are not yet met
Continue to manage ongoing symptoms on clinical grounds regardless of an early low troponin (see urgent findings)

rationale: A single value rarely confirms or excludes MI — the rise/fall pattern on the validated local pathway (0/1-hour, 0/2-hour or other) is central to interpretation
Dynamic ECG change can appear after an initial normal ECG and is central to identifying ongoing ischaemia alongside troponin trend
Identifies significant anaemia as a contributor to a type 2 (supply–demand) troponin rise
Renal impairment is associated with chronic troponin elevation and is relevant context when interpreting an abnormal result
Supports assessment for heart failure when a raised troponin occurs alongside breathlessness or signs of fluid overload
Relevant when pulmonary embolism is a differential for a raised troponin with hypoxia, tachycardia or pleuritic chest pain
